t: Sound: why it is meant to sound natural
x: Sound: why it is meant to sound natural The first synth used bare oscillators: a sine flute, a sawtooth harmonium, a plain tone for the strings. That is why songs sounded electronic. Each instrument is now a small physical model (web web/synth.js , Android lib/synth.dart , same design). Instrument Model Tanpura, veena Karplus-Strong plucked string: a delay loop with loss, so the attack and the fade of the highs are real; a soft clip stands in for the jawari bridge, bright at first and mellowing as the string quietens. A veena meend is a real slide of the sounding string. Bansuri A blown tube: strong fundamental, weak overtones, a chiff of air at the start, breath noise through the note, vibrato that begins after the note, slow pitch drift, an unslurred note scooped up into pitch. Harmonium Reed spectrum, two reed banks slightly out of tune plus an octave bank, uneven bellows pressure, wooden body resonances at 700 and 2100 Hz. Tabla Dayan: Sa with harmonic partials that decay at different rates, skin slap and rim click. Bayan: a boom whose pitch rises, a wet thud, a muted ka. No two strokes the same. Manjira Brass cymbals (inharmonic partials), soft, on the beat in devotional songs (web). Room A stereo impulse response with pre-delay and early reflections, and a tail that darkens as it fades. Master Soft tape-style saturation, a gentle top-end roll-off, a low shelf, compressor and limiter. Playing Timing jitter of a few milliseconds, velocity variation, and a dynamic arc: a quiet alap that grows, a gat that swells and settles with each phrase, a strong tihai. Measured (45 s of the same bhajan score, old synth against new, against 5 reference tracks in ~/library ) old new reference tracks 95% of energy below 345 Hz 620 Hz 410 to 880 Hz Spectral flatness (richness) 0.004 0.025 0.007 to 0.049 Loudness range, 1 s windows 3.9 dB 8 dB 5 to 16 dB These are numbers about timbre and dynamics. The reference recordings were only measured, never copied or sampled. Mix balance (measured, 80 s of the bhajan, alap and gat) Rendering each part alone showed the tanpura 20 dB under the flute, so the drone was almost inaudible. I raised it 10 dB. Now: the tanpura is about 11 dB under the flute, the tabla about 3 dB under it, and the overall level is unchanged. The flute leads, the drone gives the floor, the tabla keeps time. Limits These are models, not recordings. They sound far less electronic than before, but a recording of a real player is still better. The way to go further is a library of properly licensed instrument samples, or a hosted music model (a GPU service). Neither is included. The voice speaks the words; it does not sing them to the melody.

x: AI voice Songs, poems, bhajans, stories, pravachan, the Speech tab and film narration use a neural voice: real audio the browser mixes with the music, instead of the device's own speech. The device voice is still there as a fallback and as a choice ("Device voice"). How it works The browser asks POST /api/tts {text, lang, style, voice} for each line (at most 320 characters). The Lambda ( api/voice.py ) looks for the audio in S3 ( tts/<hash>.wav ). A hit is free and shared by every user. A miss calls an OpenRouter audio model with a strict "read this text word for word, add nothing" prompt, wraps the PCM as a 24 kHz WAV, stores it, and returns its URL. The browser ( neural.js ) downloads and decodes the WAV and schedules it with WebAudio: reverb shared with the raga, the music ducked 8 dB under each line, a limiter on the output, no two lines overlapping (a late line is nudged after the previous one; a long line is sped up at most 20%). If anything fails (no key, daily cap, offline, a line that will not generate) that line is spoken by the device voice, so nothing goes silent. Downloaded MP3 and WAV files now include the AI voice, and so does the film WebM export. The Android player does the same natively ( lib/player.dart ): it fetches the lines, plays them on a second player, and ducks the music. Models and cost Devotional and poem text ( bhajan , song , poem , pravachan ) uses openai/gpt-audio , about $0.005 per spoken line. Stories, explainers, the Speech tab and film narration use openai/gpt-audio-mini , about $0.0003 per line. If the mini model returns audio far longer than the text should take (it once added extra sentences), the line is redone on the full model. The whole build and test of this feature, with retries, cost about $0.51. Caps (environment variables, defaults): TTS_USER_DAILY_USD=0.60 per user per day, TTS_SITE_DAILY_USD=12 for the whole site per day. Only new generations count; cached lines are free. Change models with TTS_MODEL and TTS_MODEL_MINI . Voices: male = onyx, female = shimmer. Measured quality (not listening) Each language was spoken, then transcribed back by a separate model call and compared with the original text: Hindi 96%, Marathi 95%, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Kannada and English 100%. The differences are mostly spelling variants, but a human who knows the language should still listen. Mix of the two sample songs, rendered offline: voice 3 to 6 dB above the ducked music, peak 0.94, no clipped samples, no overlapping lines. Limits It speaks, it does not sing to the melody. t: Physics, auto-tune, GAN phrases and the shared studio
x: Physics, auto-tune, GAN phrases and the shared studio Song engine (music_engine_framework_layer/mhraaga_engine) compose() builds the raga score from grammar (alap, gat, tihai), then three stages shape it: GAN phrases ( gan.py ). A small generative adversarial network (generator 6-16-8, discriminator 8-16-1) trained on about 1,800 eight-note phrases harvested from the grammar of every classical raga, a sample of melakartas and gopi ragas ( agentic/train_gan.py , numpy, offline). Weights ship in gan_weights.json ; inference is plain Python so the Lambda needs no numpy. About 30% of gat phrases come from the generator, snapped to the raga's own notes so they cannot leave the raga. Honest limit: it learns the grammar's phrase shapes, not taste. After training the discriminator scores real and generated phrases about equally (0.5), so its score is a weak filter, not a quality judge. Physics ( physics.py ). Runs on the real Box2D engine (pybox2d 2.3.10, the C++ library) wherever it can be imported, which is the deployed Lambda (python3.12, x86_64; the wheel is fetched by deploy.sh ). It drives: rubato (a body on a Box2D wheel-joint spring, kicked by phrase endings and sampled at the next note; at most 28 ms, about 10 ms in practice), weight (a ball dropped under gravity onto an edge fixture with restitution; the speed at impact sets the dynamic, so leaps strike harder, and stressed vadi/samvadi notes are heavier), meend glide time (a critically damped spring whose mass grows with the interval, 0.15 to 0.25 s) and a slow pitch wander . If Box2D cannot be imported (a laptop without the wheel) the same models run on a small pure-Python solver using the same algorithms; the two agree to about 1 ms. Every score records which one ran in meta.physics.engine . The tihai is never moved, so the last note lands exactly on sam. Auto-tune ( autotune.py ). Pulls every lead note toward the nearest in-raga shruti (just intonation) by 75%, and hard-snaps the tihai. It also offers track() for a recorded pitch track with a dead-band that keeps vibrato. Notes are now [time, hz, duration, ornament, velocity, glide] . Old four-field scores still play. compose(..., human=False) turns physics off. The score's meta.physics reports what was applied. The web synth, the offline MP3 export and the Android synth all read velocity. Shared studio (api/team.py, web/team.html, web/team.js) One film or song project, up to 150 people and 300 layers. A layer is one film shot or one song section, owned by one artist. Role Can director everything: add or remove people, reorder, approve, render, delete the project artist create (up to 8) and edit only their own layers, set them to review, comment viewer read and comment Conflicts: every layer save carries the revision it was based on. If someone changed the layer first the save fails with 409 and the editor reloads their version. Nobody overwrites anyone silently. x: Pecova Many Agents. Adaptive Intelligence. One Outcome. Pecova is the backend engine behind Algo aKANADE's integrations — external products (starting with Outreach-Ai ) that call Kalkee's APIs to get model access, routing, and (eventually) their own spawned agents, without needing their own LLM infrastructure. Outreach-Ai → AI integration layer (API + cache) → Kalkee APIs → Pecova Kalkee is the backend. Pecova is the backend engine : the thing that actually decides which model answers a given request, and — for integrations that opt into it — runs and tracks the agents doing the work. PECOVA PE Parallel Execution C Collaboration O Orchestration V Versatile Intelligence A Adaptation Multiple specialized agents and models collaborate, tasks are routed intelligently, results are evaluated, and the system adapts through feedback — without any exploration/bandit algorithm making that adaptation non-deterministic or hard to explain. x: Kalkee — Explained: What, How, and the Code Line by Line This is the "explain it to me" document — no arrow diagrams (see README_ARROW_DIAGRAMS.md ), no formula reference (see README_RL_ALGORITHMS.md ). Just: what is "intent," what is RAG, how does the RL primitive actually work at the code level, and what does each layer in this system actually do and why. What is "intent," in this system? "Intent" is what perceive_intent (step 6 of the 17-step algorithm) figures out: which single tool the user's message is actually asking for, with what arguments — or, if none fit, that the message doesn't map to any PM action at all. Concretely: the LLM is given the full list of available tools (their names, descriptions, and argument schemas) alongside the conversation, and asked to either (a) call exactly one tool with extracted arguments, or (b) reply in plain text if nothing fits. That's the entirety of "understanding intent" here — it is deliberately not a general free-form reasoning step. The model isn't asked "what should happen next in the abstract"; it's asked "which of these specific, pre-defined actions (if any) does this map to." That narrowness is what makes output_guard possible at all: a tool call's shape can be mechanically validated against a known JSON schema, and entity names can be mechanically resolved against real data (step 7) rather than trusted as-is — the model's job is classification + extraction, not open-ended generation. When nothing fits, that's out_of_scope: true — a real signal, not an error. The system doesn't refuse; it answers as best it can in free text, but flags that answer as "general knowledge, not grounded in your PM data," and the UI gates showing it behind an explicit "show me anyway." What is RAG, and why does this system have two versions of it? RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation. The core idea, in one sentence: instead of asking a language model to answer purely from whatever it memorized during training, you first retrieve a handful of relevant text passages from a knowledge base you control, hand those passages to the model as extra context, and ask it to answer grounded in that context . This matters for two reasons: the model's training data is frozen at some past date and doesn't know about your data at all (your tasks, your documents), and grounding an answer in retrieved text makes it checkable — you can point at exactly which passage backed a claim, instead of trusting an ungrounded assertion. The mechanics, step by step: Chunk — a long document is split into smaller passages ( rag.py 's chunk_text() ), because embedding and retrieving whole documents is both less precise and more expensive than retrieving the specific paragraph that actually answers the question. Embed — each chunk is converted into a vector (a list of numbers) that captures its meaning, such that semantically similar chunks end up as nearby vectors. This system uses either a real sentence- embedding model or, when that's not installed

t: Provider budgets — daily token/cost caps, with automatic fallback
x: Provider budgets — daily token/cost caps, with automatic fallback The problem this solves: an admin adds a real API key for a paid provider (Claude is the motivating case, but this applies to ANY provider with a real per-token cost — Groq, an admin-added OpenRouter model, anything) and now has no way to cap what it can spend. A single runaway session, a bug in a client, or just normal usage growth can run up a real bill with no ceiling. llm/provider_budget.py closes that gap: set a daily token limit and/or a daily dollar limit for any provider, and once either is hit, that provider is automatically excluded from the fallback chain for the rest of the day — the exact same "just try the next rung" mechanism a real provider outage already takes, so a maxed-out budget degrades gracefully instead of erroring or silently overspending. How it works Real chat turn arrives │ ▼ TierClient.chat() builds the candidate chain for this tier │ ▼ For each candidate provider key: provs[key].available() ── base_url/api_key present? AND NOT provider_budget.is_exceeded(key) ── today's usage under both caps? │ ▼ Only providers passing BOTH checks are tried, in order — an explicit "preferred" pick (Domain mode, Hybrid mode, or a user's own model choice) gets the SAME check, so an admin capping "claude" can't be bypassed by picking it directly. │ ▼ A call succeeds → its real usage (prompt_tokens + completion_tokens, from the provider's own response) is recorded against today's running total for that provider. │ ▼ Next call: if the running total now meets or exceeds either configured cap, this same provider is excluded — automatically, no admin action, no restart. │ ▼ UTC midnight: a new day's usage row starts at zero — the provider is available again with no manual reset. Token caps work with zero extra configuration — every provider that reports usage ( LLMResult.usage ) already has real numbers to check against. Cost caps need an admin-supplied $/1k-token rate (there's no live pricing feed built in for every possible provider) — setting a max_cost_usd without also giving at least one of cost_per_1k_prompt_tokens / cost_per_1k_completion_tokens is rejected outright, rather than silently accepting a cap that could never mathematically trip. Using it From the Admin UI : Admin > AI Models > "Provider budgets" — + Add budget , enter the provider key ( claude for the built-in Claude rung, or the exact name of an admin-added model above), a max tokens/day and/or max cost/day, and (for a cost cap) the real $/1k rates from that provider's own pricing page. The table shows each provider's today's usage and whether it's currently OK or Exceeded , live — no refresh needed beyond the page's own poll. Export CSV on that table downloads the current caps + usage snapshot. From the API ( app/routers/admin_provider_budgets.py , Executive-role only, same bar as admin_providers.py since this configures spend against a real key): # Cap the built-in Claude rung at 500k tokens/day curl -X

This complements README_ARROW_DIAGRAMS.md (pictures, no math) and README_EXPLAINED.md (prose, line-by-line code walkthrough). Worth knowing if you're comparing against other routers/gateways : OpenRouter's own docs describe deterministic price/latency-weighted provider selection, and LiteLLM's router picks from explicit named strategies (least-busy, cost-based) — neither maintains a learned posterior that updates from real outcomes the way every algorithm below does. CrewAI and AutoGen/AG2 have no built-in adaptive routing either (the "RL" that turns up searching either one is a separate external training project, not a native routing capability). See README.md 's "How Kalkee compares" table for the full picture. 0. The formal objective everything below approximates Reinforcement learning, in general, seeks a policy π maximizing expected discounted return: π* = argmax_π E[ Σ_t γ^t R_t ] Every bandit in this codebase is the γ → 0 special case: a single decision, one immediate reward, no multi-step planning. That's a deliberate scope choice (see gmaofn/router.py 's module docstring) — a full MDP solver (Q-learning, PPO) over an entire multi-turn task is the natural next step and is left as a pluggable strategy, not implemented twice. The one place this repo does something genuinely closer to full RL is the nightly PEFT fine-tune (§7 below), which updates real model weights rather than picking between existing options. 1. The shared primitive — linear contextual bandit via Thompson Sampling Source: Agrawal & Goyal, "Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits with Linear Payoffs," ICML 2013. Implemented once in gmaofn/bandit.py 's LinearBanditCore , reused by every layer in §2-§6 below. Model. For each arm a , maintain a Bayesian linear regression posterior over "reward given context vector x": reward | x ~ N(θ_aᵗx, σ²) θ_a ~ N(μ_a, ν² B_a⁻¹) State kept per arm (accumulated from every past (x, reward) pair that arm has actually received): B_a = Σ x xᵗ + λI (λ = ridge prior strength — LinearBanditCore's `ridge`) f_a = Σ r·x μ_a = B_a⁻¹ f_a (posterior mean) Selecting an arm ( LinearBanditCore.select ): for every candidate arm, sample a fresh weight vector from its own posterior and score the current context against it — θ̃_a ~ N(μ_a, ν² B_a⁻¹) (ν = exploration_scale) choose argmax_a θ̃_a · x Sampling — rather than always using μ_a directly — is what gives Thompson Sampling its exploration: an arm with a wide (uncertain) posterior occasionally wins even when its mean looks worse, so it keeps collecting data instead of being starved by one early bad outcome. As more (x, reward) pairs accumulate, B_a grows, the posterior narrows, and the sampled θ̃_a converges toward the true μ_a. Updating after an outcome ( LinearBanditCore.update ): B_a ← B_a + x xᵗ f_a ← f_a + r·x Cold start. ensure() seeds a brand-new arm's posterior mean at a hand

Lyrics are timed to the phrases. The feel. Real physics makes it human: a Box2D spring gives rubato, a falling ball gives each note its weight, another spring gives the meend glide. Your device plays it with physical models: plucked-string tanpura, breathy bansuri, reed harmonium, tabla from its modes, a room reverb, human timing and dynamics. The voice. Each lyric line is spoken by a neural voice model. The audio is made once, stored in S3 and shared by everyone, so the second listener pays nothing and waits nothing. The browser lays the voice over the music, turns the music down under each line, and runs a limiter so nothing clips. Downloads (MP3 or WAV) include the voice.
